planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; seed benefits from a period of cold moist stratification over winter if sown in fall.

directions: Engelmann's milkweed is a slender, upright Great Plains and Texas native with narrow, grass-like leaves and small clusters of greenish-cream flowers in summer, serving as both a monarch and queen butterfly host plant where it occurs naturally. It thrives in lean, rocky, or sandy well-drained soil and tolerates considerable drought once established, making it a good fit for xeric native plantings. Grow in full sun; it resents heavy, wet, or richly amended garden soil, which can shorten its lifespan. Established plants form a deep taproot and resent transplanting, so site divisions or seedlings in a permanent spot.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant in spring into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; a high-elevation Rocky Mountain native that benefits from winter cold stratification before germinating.

directions: Hall's milkweed is an uncommon, high-elevation native of the central and southern Rocky Mountains, bearing clusters of rose-pink flowers above narrow, lance-shaped leaves on a compact upright plant. It is adapted to gritty, well-drained mountain soils and full sun, tolerating cold winters and short growing seasons far better than lowland milkweed species. Like other Asclepias it forms an important nectar and larval host for monarch butterflies within its range, though it remains uncommon in cultivation. Grow it in a rock garden or native alpine-meadow planting with sharp drainage, since it does not tolerate heavy, wet soil.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; native to Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona grasslands and desert grassland edges.

directions: Nodding milkweed carries broad, blue-green, waxy leaves and rounded clusters of bronze-green to purplish flowers that droop slightly on their stalks, giving the species its common name. Native to dry grasslands and desert grassland edges of the southwestern US and northern Mexico, it tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline soils better than many eastern milkweed species. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect a long, deep taproot once established that makes mature plants resent being moved. It serves as a larval host for monarch and queen butterflies within its native range.

common_name: Charlotte's Blush Tropical Milkweed (Variegated Pink-and-Cream Foliage)

planting.note: Transplant after last frost in full sun; this variegated sport is grown as a perennial in zones 9-11 or as a tender annual elsewhere. In mild-winter climates where it survives year-round, cut plants back hard in late fall/winter to interrupt the OE parasite cycle in overwintering monarchs, and consider native regional milkweed species as the primary planting instead.

directions: Charlotte's Blush is a stable variegated sport of tropical milkweed discovered in Florida, with leaves and seed pods streaked in cream, pink, and green rather than the plain green of the species. It flowers continuously through the warm season with the same orange-and-yellow blooms as common tropical milkweed, serving as a nectar source and larval host for monarch butterflies. Tropical milkweed is native to the Caribbean and South America, not North America, and in mild-winter regions where it fails to die back naturally it has been linked to year-round monarch breeding and higher rates of the protozoan parasite OE (Ophryocystis elektroscirrha); gardeners in zones 9-11 are often advised to cut it to the ground each winter or choose a regional native Asclepias species instead. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and expect self-seeding where winters stay mild.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated divisions, never wild-collected material, in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this species is critically imperiled in the wild and extremely rare in the nursery trade.

directions: Basil mountain mint is one of the rarest species in its genus, known from only a handful of sites in the eastern US and considered critically imperiled by conservation authorities. Like its more common mountain mint relatives it bears dense clusters of small white flowers in summer that are highly attractive to a wide range of pollinating insects, held above aromatic, basil-scented foliage. Because of its extreme rarity, source plants only from reputable nurseries propagating from cultivated stock, never from wild populations. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade as a conservation planting rather than a mainstream garden perennial.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the only Pycnanthemum species native west of the Rockies, found in California foothill and mountain seeps.

directions: Sierra mountain mint is a geographically disjunct western outlier of an otherwise eastern North American genus, occurring naturally in moist seeps, streambanks, and foothill woodlands of California. It produces the same dense clusters of small white flowers typical of mountain mints, drawing large numbers of bees, wasps, and butterflies over a long summer bloom period, above strongly aromatic foliage. Grow in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where it can spread modestly by rhizomes without crowding smaller companions. It is a useful, under-planted pollinator perennial for California native gardens seeking an alternative to eastern mountain mint species.

common_name: Burgundy Blast False Indigo (Dark Wine-Purple Color-Break Baptisia)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a Baptisia minor x Baptisia alba cross bred by Walters Gardens, first sold in 2021.

directions: Burgundy Blast breaks from the usual blue, white, or yellow Baptisia flower palette with dark wine-purple spires rising above blue-green, clover-like foliage in late spring. Like other false indigos it develops a deep taproot that makes it extremely drought-tolerant once established and resentful of transplanting, so choose a permanent site from the start. It is a long-lived, low-maintenance native perennial that draws bumblebees and other pollinators to its pea-like flowers, followed by decorative seed pods that rattle in late summer wind. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid heavy, wet ground, which can rot the thick roots.

common_name: Prairie Princess Hybrid Ironweed (Compact Proven Winners Vernonia)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; a compact Proven Winners hybrid ironweed bred for garden-scale use rather than the towering height of wild Vernonia species.

directions: Prairie Princess is a compact hybrid ironweed selected to stay well under half the height of wild Vernonia species while keeping the same clusters of small, rich purple flowers that late-season pollinators, especially bees and butterflies, rely on heavily. Its reduced stature removes the main objection gardeners have to ironweed in a border setting, fitting into mixed perennial plantings without flopping or needing support. Grow in full sun in moist to average, well-drained soil, and expect reliable fall bloom when many other perennials have finished. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain a tidy, floriferous habit.
